chapters: Words as maps: how AI captures meaning

units.t: Artificial Intelligence. Episode two.
In this episode: How computers learned to see, Words as maps: how AI captures meaning and How AI chatbots work.
Part one. How computers learned to see.
To a computer, a photo of your dog is just a grid of numbers.
Teaching machines to find the dog in those numbers took sixty years, millions of labelled images and one famous breakthrough.
Why seeing is hard.
In 1966, researchers at MIT launched the Summer Vision Project, hoping students could build a significant part of an object-recognition system in one summer.
It became a famous example of underestimating a problem.
Seeing feels effortless to us, so it seemed easy.
But a computer sees an image only as a grid of numbers recording the brightness and colour of each pixel.
Photograph your cat in the morning, at night under a lamp, and curled up from above.
To you it is the same cat, yet to a computer the images share almost no pixel values.
Early systems used hand-designed rules for edges and corners.
They could read printed text but struggled with the real world.
Learning to see in layers.
The approach that won out was to let the computer learn its own features.
Convolutional neural networks, developed in the late 1980s by researchers including Yann LeCun, scan an image with small filters, each looking for a pattern wherever it appears.
Early layers spot simple things like edges and patches of colour.
Later layers combine these into textures and shapes, such as fur, eyes or wheels, and the final layers recognise whole objects.
Nobody tells the network what to look for; it discovers features by adjusting itself during training.
An early success was reading handwritten digits, and the technology read cheques automatically in the 1990s.
But it needed far more data and computing power to truly shine.
ImageNet and the big bang.
In the late 2000s, Fei-Fei Li and her colleagues built an enormous collection of labelled photos.
ImageNet eventually held over fourteen million images in thousands of categories, labelled with the help of crowdsourced workers online.
From 2010, an annual contest challenged teams to classify its photos.
In 2012, a University of Toronto team including Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton entered a deep convolutional network trained on graphics chips designed for video games.
It slashed the error rate far below its rivals.
This moment, often called the start of the deep learning revolution, convinced much of the AI field to switch to neural networks almost overnight.
Fooled by stickers.
Vision systems can fail in ways no human would.
Adding a carefully calculated pattern of noise, invisible to the eye, can make a network confidently mistake a panda for something else.
These are called adversarial examples.
Later experiments showed that a few strategically placed stickers on a stop sign could cause some systems to misread it.
Networks can also latch onto shortcuts, recognising cows partly because they usually appear on grass, then failing to spot a cow on a beach.
These quirks suggest networks don't see the world as we do.
They find patterns that work most of the time, but can break under unusual conditions.
Vision everywhere, faces and fairness.
Computer vision quietly unlocks phones, sharpens photos, blurs video-call backgrounds, reads number plates and checks factory products for defects.

In Australian agriculture it spots weeds so herbicide can be targeted precisely, and conservation researchers use it to sort millions of camera-trap photos, identifying animals from quolls to feral cats.
Facial recognition is the controversial use.
Some systems have been less accurate for women and people with darker skin, often because training data was unbalanced, and a false match can seriously harm an innocent person.
There is also privacy: being identified and tracked in a crowd is very different from being seen.
In Australia, a faceprint is sensitive information under privacy law, and the Information Commissioner has found some businesses' use of facial recognition breached privacy rules.
The key idea: A computer sees only a grid of numbers, and the same object can produce completely different numbers.
Part two. Words as maps: how AI captures meaning.
Computers only understand numbers.
So how can a machine know that 'puppy' is close to 'dog' and far from 'spreadsheet'?
The answer is to give every word a place on a giant map.
The company words keep.
In 1957 the linguist J. R. Firth wrote: 'You shall know a word by the company it keeps.'
You can learn a lot about a word from its neighbours.
Meet 'wombok' in 'the wombok was crisp and fresh' and 'she chopped the wombok for the stir-fry', and you'd guess it's a vegetable.
'Coffee' and 'tea' both appear near 'cup', 'hot' and 'morning'.
Computers need numbers, but the simplest scheme, numbering each word, fails.
'Aardvark' is 1, 'abacus' is 2, and the numbers carry no meaning: to such a system 'cat' and 'kitten' are as unrelated as 'cat' and 'carburettor'.
Better to give related words related numbers, so what a model learns about 'dog' transfers to 'puppy'.
A map of meaning.
The solution is an embedding: a list of numbers, often a few hundred long, acting as coordinates that place each word on an enormous map.
An ordinary map needs two numbers; an embedding uses hundreds of dimensions we can't picture, but the mathematics works the same way.
'Sydney', 'Melbourne' and 'Brisbane' cluster in one region, 'happy', 'glad' and 'cheerful' in another.
People don't choose the positions.
The model learns them from huge amounts of text.
In 2013 a Google team led by Tomas Mikolov released word2vec.
Directions on the map seemed to carry meaning: 'king' minus 'man' plus 'woman' landed nearest 'queen'.
The famous examples were somewhat selected, and the arithmetic is less neat in general, but meaning had been captured in geometry.
Learning our biases too.
Because embeddings learn from human writing, they also learn human prejudices.
In 2016 researchers showed that word2vec embeddings trained on news articles completed analogies such as 'man is to computer programmer as woman is to homemaker'.
In 2017 another team found that embeddings reproduced many associations measured in psychological tests of human bias, linking some names, genders and groups with pleasant or unpleasant words.
The embeddings weren't programmed to be biased; they faithfully mapped the patterns in their text.
This matters because embeddings sit inside search engines, recruitment tools and recommendation systems, where such associations can quietly shape real decisions.
Researchers have developed methods to measure and reduce these effects.
Same word, new meaning.
The original embeddings gave each word one fixed position.
But 'bank' means something different in 'river bank' and 'bank loan', and 'bat' could be an animal or cricket gear.
One point has to blur these together.
From around 2018, new models, soon dominated by the transformer design, began producing contextual embeddings, where a word's position is recalculated for each sentence using every surrounding word.
Today's chatbots work this way.
Text is broken into pieces called tokens, each starting with an embedding, and many layers then refine them, mixing in context until the model has a rich representation of the whole passage.
Maps of everything.
The embedding idea spread far beyond single words.
Whole sentences and documents can be embedded, so a search engine can find pages matching the meaning of your question even if they share no exact words with it.
Songs, products and films can be embedded based on who enjoys them, helping recommendation systems suggest similar items.
Some systems embed images and text into the same shared space, so a photo of a beach lands near the words 'sand and waves', letting you search your photo library by description.
Whenever an app finds things that are 'similar' in a way that feels like understanding, there is a good chance it is measuring distances on a learned map.
The key idea: Words used in similar contexts have similar meanings, so giving words arbitrary ID numbers tells a computer nothing.
Part three. How AI chatbots work.
They can write essays and code, yet they sometimes invent facts with total confidence.
Understanding how they work explains both.
Predicting the next word.
Chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are built on large language models, or LLMs.
At their core they do something that sounds simple: given some text, they predict what text is likely to come next.
They generate replies one small piece at a time, called a token, which is often part of a word.
Each token is predicted from everything before it.
Done extremely well, at enormous scale, this produces surprisingly capable writing, reasoning and conversation.
Learning from text.
A model is trained on a huge collection of text, such as books, websites and code.
It repeatedly tries to predict missing or next words and adjusts itself when it's wrong, tuning billions of internal numbers called parameters.
Over trillions of examples it picks up grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and writing styles.
Nobody writes explicit rules; the patterns are learned from data.
Modern models use the transformer, introduced by Google researchers in a 2017 paper, 'Attention Is All You Need'.
Its key idea, attention, lets the model weigh how every word relates to every other, so it can track context, like what 'it' refers to several sentences back.
ChatGPT's release in November 2022 brought this technology to the public.
Becoming helpful.
A model trained only to predict text isn't automatically a helpful assistant.
It might just continue your question with more questions.
So developers fine-tune it on examples of good conversations.
They also use feedback, often from people rating different answers, to reward responses that are helpful, honest and harmless.
This technique is known as reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF, along with variations of it.
It's also how developers try to reduce harmful or biased outputs.
Confident but wrong.
Because language models generate what sounds plausible, they can give confident, fluent answers that are simply wrong, including made-up facts, quotes, statistics or references.
This is called hallucination.
Unless connected to search tools, a model isn't looking things up in a database of facts.
Newer systems hallucinate less and can cite sources, but errors still happen, especially on obscure topics, precise numbers and recent events.
Models also don't read letters as you do.
Text is chopped into tokens, so 'strawberry' may arrive as a couple of chunks, which is one reason chatbots famously miscounted its r's.
Newer 'reasoning' models work step by step and have improved greatly at maths and logic, but fluency in one area says little about reliability in another.
Limits and the bigger picture.
A language model doesn't update its knowledge while you chat.
What it knows comes from data collected up to a cut-off date, so without a search tool it may not know recent news or prices.
It can also only consider a limited amount of text at once, its context window.
Modern windows hold hundreds of pages, but very long chats can still lose early details.
Some apps add 'memory' features, which can usually be viewed and switched off in settings.
AI also raises big questions: jobs, convincing fake images and video, energy and water use, responsibility for harm, and safety.
Governments, including Australia's, are developing rules.
Understanding the basics helps you use these tools wisely.
The key idea: AI chatbots generate text by repeatedly predicting the most likely next token, based on everything before it.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why can the same cat look completely different to a computer?
Answer. Light, angle and position change the pixel numbers.
Question two. Why is numbering words 1, 2, 3 a poor way to give them to a computer?
Answer. The numbers say nothing about meaning.
Question three. What is the core task of a large language model?
Answer. Predicting what text is likely to come next.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
